stances.claim: To be effective as a corporate director in post-retirement, CJ has had to learn the digital tools of millennials -- smartphones, then artificial intelligence, blockchain, and internet of things -- recognizing these three as the technologies that will shape the near future and require directors to keep pace.
stances.rhetorical_move: adaptation-as-duty framing (directors must learn or become obsolete)

stances.claim: The PH tycoon successions CJ has witnessed firsthand demonstrate that the young heirs (Jaime Augusto and Fernando Ayala, Arthur and Alfred Ty, Lance Gokongwei, Piki Lopez, Tessie Sy Coson) inherited not just the wealth but the hard work, grit, and ingenuity of the old -- and crucially the drive to help build the nation's economy and wellbeing.

The most amazing entrepreneurs CJ has met are Manuel V. Pangilinan (who managed MVP Group's phoenix-like rise from the 1998 real estate debacle to unqualified current success) and Ramon S. Ang (who parlayed San Miguel from a modest food/beer processor to a multifaceted behemoth) -- singling them out by name as the apex business builders of the post-2006 era.

CJ's three-criteria board decline rule -- unavoidable meeting conflicts, direct competitor conflicts, uncomfortable corporate cultures -- is the principal discipline that makes 100% column writing + full board attendance possible alongside retirement, and is replicable by anyone facing multiple-engagement decisions.

notable_anecdotes: CJ's smartphone-to-AI/blockchain/IoT trajectory at retirement age -- explicitly framed as 'the new tools of millennials' that a post-retirement director must learn -- making the column unusually candid about technological self-modernization in old age.

The Felipe Gozon anecdote: 'a compañero I had crossed swords with since the 1970s who got me to the board of GMA 7 in early 2007. By the way, I asked him several times to join the Court, but he preferred to oversee the phenomenal growth of the multibillion-peso Kapuso network' -- capturing both their 40+ year relationship and the road-not-taken counterfactual.

The Dasmariñas Village price arc -- 1979 purchase at P2,000/sqm, current P400,000/sqm -- the most concrete personal-wealth illustration of PH real estate appreciation in any CJ column, using own home as the example.
Manila Polo Club proprietary membership at P100,000 (then) and P23 million (now); Manila Golf at P200K then and P60M now -- another concrete personal-asset appreciation curve.

CJ's commitment of half his retirement pay to the FLP -- the most consequential single charitable commitment in his post-retirement portrait, demonstrating skin-in-the-game for the liberty-and-prosperity philosophy.

Taipans consulting CJ on 'how to deploy more effectively their private wealth to philanthropy' -- the most quietly significant role disclosed in the column, positioning CJ as informal philanthropy advisor to PH's wealthiest.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban continues his retirement-thanksgiving series by chronicling his concurrent careers as corporate director/adviser and foundation trustee/officer since leaving the Supreme Court in 2006. To be effective, he has had to learn the millennials' tools -- from smartphones to the three technologies he flags as shaping the near future: artificial intelligence, blockchain, and internet of things -- using his directorship at Metro Pacific Investments (14 hospitals including Makati Med and Asian Hospital) for cutting-edge medical knowledge. He portrays the tycoon successions he has witnessed firsthand: Jaime Zobel de Ayala to Jaime Augusto and Fernando; George S.K. Ty to Arthur and Alfred; John Gokongwei Jr. (and James) to Lance; Oscar M. Lopez to Piki; and Henry Sy Sr. to Tessie and siblings -- with the young heirs inheriting not just wealth but 'the hard work, grit and ingenuity of the old' plus the drive to build the nation. He names Tony Tan Caktiong (Jollibee from solitary eatery to Asia's largest QSR) and Edgar 'Injap' Sia (Mang Inasal, Double Dragon) as the newest taipans he has met, and singles out Manuel V. Pangilinan (MVP Group's phoenix-like rise from the 1998 real estate debacle) and Ramon S. Ang (San Miguel from food/beer to multifaceted behemoth) as 'the most amazing entrepreneurs.' He shares his discipline -- strict time management, declining boards with meeting conflicts, direct-competitor conflicts, or uncomfortable cultures (singling out Japanese and Emirati work ethic as exemplary) -- and his stock-market investment criteria (profitability, growth, public float, transparency, trustworthiness, governance, social responsibility). He illustrates real-estate appreciation with his own Dasmariñas Village purchase (P2,000/sqm in 1979 → P400,000/sqm now) and proprietary memberships in Manila Polo (P100K → P23M) and Manila Golf (P200K → P60M). He closes on philanthropy: half his retirement pay committed to the FLP, his service to the Manila Cathedral Foundation, the Metrobank Foundation, and the Tan Yan Kee Foundation, plus consultations from taipans on 'how to deploy more effectively their private wealth to philanthropy.'
